And it has opened up the possibility for more research, as Sobel and his team will now be able to experiment more with the wearable device they developed, reports Scientific American. 

“It goes to show,” Gane tells Popular Science, “that we need to take olfaction a bit more seriously.”

More than three decades ago, amphibian researchers from around the globe converged on Canterbury, England, for the first World Congress of Herpetology—and, over drinks, shared the same frightening tale. 

Frogs were disappearing in the wild, and no one could explain why. 

It was “a scary time,” recalls Australian veterinary scientist Lee Berger, who in the 1990s was one of the first to identify the culprit: a water-borne chytrid fungus known as Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis, or Bd. 

Scientists know now that the stealthy menace originated in East Asia and was probably spread inadvertently by people to every continent except Antarctica. 

The parasitic fungus can be as transmissible as it is lethal, wiping out entire populations of some frogs in a matter of weeks. And until recently it has proved largely unstoppable. Despite more than 25 years of intense study, conservationists haven’t devised a panacea that can prevent Bd infections or save populations of frogs after they contract the Bd-caused skin disease chytridiomycosis. 

Bd has been implicated in the decline and possible extinction of around 200 frog species. 

Yet today, Berger and other researchers see grounds for optimism. There’s evidence that some frogs are naturally evolving resistance. Scientists are also trying to exploit the fungus’s sensitivity to temperature by building Bd-free habitats or moving frogs to locales where the fungus can’t survive. Still others are investigating viruses that attack Bd and eventually might be used to reduce its virulence. These innovative strategies are emerging like slimy glimmers of hope on an otherwise gloomy landscape. 

Chytridiomycosis kills because skin is an integral part of a frog’s cardiovascular system. When chytrid fungus colonizes the skin, electrolytes can’t get absorbed. This disrupts the heart’s electrical rhythms, and the animals die of heart failure. 

But though ruthlessly efficient at killing off some frog species, the fungus is highly vulnerable to heat: Temperatures above 30 degrees Celsius (about 85 degrees Fahrenheit) slow disease progression. 

The armored mist frog in the Wet Tropics of Queensland, Australia, appears to have shifted habitats, allowing it to take advantage of this fungal Achilles’ heel. The frog—thought extinct for almost 20 years—no longer dwells in shaded areas near the forest’s mountain waterfalls. But a population persists in warmer, sun-drenched areas. Perhaps that’s because the frogs can rest on sunbaked rocks through the night, which elevates their body temperatures enough to stave off Bd, says biologist Conrad Hoskin of James Cook University in Queensland. 

Since 2013, Hoskin has been transplanting armored mist frogs from the surviving population into new, similarly sunny habitats and closely monitoring the health of these new colonies. 

In a larger effort, Hoskin and colleagues recently assessed the habitat ranges of 55 eastern Australian frog species, including 25 affected by Bd. They found that even though the fungus has curtailed the ranges of afflicted species, they are persisting in warmer lower elevations with more rain. 

Other researchers have also tried moving groups of Bd-infected frogs, either to salvage dying populations or to spread recovering ones. Of 15 relocations attempted in Australia over the last 20-odd years, seven populations are holding on and three are thriving. 

Providing frogs with amenities has also helped. Conservation biologist Anthony Waddle of Macquarie University in Sydney built heat shelters from large bricks prefabricated with holes that just happen to be the perfect size for green and golden bell frogs. Sick frogs that hung out in these “frog saunas” had lower infection loads than those that convalesced in the shade, Waddle and colleagues reported in 2024 in Nature. 

As this incremental progress continues, scientists are racing to figure out why some frog species are more susceptible to Bd than others. Conservation biologist Tiffany Kosch, who works with Berger at the One Health Research Group at the University of Melbourne veterinary school, is taking a genetic approach. Kosch recently sequenced the genome of the southern corroboree—a black and brilliantly yellow frog of which 50 or fewer survive in the wild. If the scientists can learn which particular versions of genes are associated with Bd resistance, they could breed and release resistant frogs, or even engineer Bd resistance into the southern corroborees. 

Researchers also have discovered a virus of fungi that appears to infect weaker strains of Bd—pathogens for the pathogen, in other words. While harnessing such viruses to help fight Bd is a long way off, it might one day be another weapon. “In the science fiction version, you spray the virus in the field and the frogs all survive—that’s the hope,” says University of California, Riverside, mycologist Jason Stajich, co-author of a recent report on the virus in Current Biology. 

Berger, who co-published an update on Australian frogs and Bd in the 2024 Annual Review of Animal Biosciences, says that that despite the losses, optimism is key to working in conservation. “You have to make a choice to focus on the positives.” 

Indeed, there’s a lot more work to be done to avoid further declines and extinctions, says ecologist Andrea Adams of the University of California, Santa Barbara. “We can’t afford to take a hands-off approach.”

As the vibrant hues of autumn sweep across Virginia's landscapes, a new initiative is ensuring that everyone can fully appreciate the seasonal spectacle. Virginia State Parks have installed specialized viewfinders equipped with lenses designed to assist individuals with red-green colorblindness, enhancing their ability to distinguish between the rich tapestry of fall colors.

Colorblindness, or color vision deficiency, affects approximately 8% of men and 0.5% of women of Northern European descent, according to the National Eye Institute. The most common form, red-green colorblindness, makes it difficult for individuals to differentiate between certain shades of red and green. This can significantly impact their experience of natural phenomena like autumn foliage, where these colors are predominant.

The new viewfinders, installed at several popular parks across the state, are equipped with EnChroma lenses. These lenses are engineered to enhance color perception by selectively filtering out certain wavelengths of light, thereby increasing the contrast between red and green hues. "Our goal is to make the beauty of Virginia's fall foliage accessible to everyone," says Dr. Emily Carter, a spokesperson for the Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation. "These viewfinders are a step towards inclusivity, allowing more visitors to experience the full spectrum of colors that nature has to offer."

The initiative is part of a broader effort to make state parks more inclusive and accessible. "We want to ensure that all visitors, regardless of their visual abilities, can enjoy the natural beauty of our parks," explains John Smith, Director of Virginia State Parks. "The installation of these viewfinders is just one of the many ways we're working to enhance the visitor experience."

The viewfinders have been strategically placed at key vantage points within the parks, offering sweeping views of the autumn landscape. Locations include the scenic overlooks at Shenandoah River State Park, the rolling hills of Grayson Highlands, and the expansive vistas of Natural Bridge State Park. These sites were chosen for their breathtaking views and the diversity of tree species, which provide a rich palette of colors during the fall season.

For individuals with colorblindness, the experience of using these viewfinders can be transformative. "It's like seeing the world in high definition for the first time," says Mark Johnson, a visitor who recently tried the viewfinder at Shenandoah River State Park. "The reds and oranges just pop in a way I've never seen before. It's truly remarkable."

Experts in the field of optometry and vision science have praised the initiative. Dr. Sarah Lin, an optometrist specializing in color vision, notes, "These viewfinders are a fantastic tool for enhancing color perception in individuals with red-green colorblindness. By filtering specific wavelengths, they allow users to perceive a broader range of colors, which can significantly enhance their visual experience."

The installation of these viewfinders comes at a perfect time, as Virginia's parks are gearing up for the annual influx of leaf-peepers—visitors who travel to view and photograph the fall foliage. The state is renowned for its stunning autumn displays, drawing tourists from across the country. With the addition of these viewfinders, Virginia is setting a precedent for other states to follow in making natural attractions more accessible to all.

As the leaves continue to change and the parks fill with visitors, the new viewfinders stand as a testament to the power of innovation and inclusivity. They offer a new way for individuals with colorblindness to connect with nature, ensuring that everyone can partake in the awe-inspiring beauty of Virginia's fall season.

In the words of Dr. Carter, "Nature's beauty is a universal gift, and it's our responsibility to ensure that everyone can enjoy it. These viewfinders are a small but significant step towards achieving that goal." As the leaves turn and the colors deepen, Virginia's parks are ready to welcome all visitors, offering a vibrant and inclusive experience for everyone.

The animal kingdom offers a captivating range when it comes to taste. The variety is remarkable, from animals with exceptional taste abilities to those that hardly perceive flavors. Recognizing these variations not only underscores how animals have adapted to their habitats but also provides clues about the evolutionary journeys that have influenced their sensory perceptions.

The Extraordinary Taste Abilities of the Catfish

Leading the taste spectrum is the catfish, an animal that can be regarded as a genuine expert in flavors. The catfish possesses the most advanced taste sense among animals, boasting more than 100,000 taste buds distributed all over its body. This extraordinary capability enables the catfish to locate food in cloudy waters with limited visibility. "A marine biologist describes catfish as being akin to mobile tongues." "Their enhanced taste sensitivity is vital for thriving in settings where other senses may not function as well."

Taste buds in catfish are spread across their skin, fins, and whisker-like barbels, rather than being limited to their mouth. This vast array of taste receptors allows the catfish to sense tiny chemical variations in the water, directing it accurately to possible food sources.

Dolphins and Their Lack of Taste Sensation

In stark contrast, dolphins possess a surprisingly underdeveloped sense of taste. In contrast to catfish, dolphins have evolved to lose the majority of their taste receptors. According to a marine mammal expert, dolphins depend mainly on their sharp hearing and echolocation for hunting and navigation. "Their taste buds are greatly diminished because taste is not essential for them."

Dolphins can still detect salt, crucial for keeping their electrolyte levels stable, but they do not have receptors for sweet, bitter, and umami tastes. This diminished sense of taste is believed to be an adaptation to their life in water, where other senses take precedence over taste.

Hummingbirds' Preference for Sweetness

Conversely, hummingbirds have developed a unique preference for sweet flavors. These small birds possess specialized taste receptors that are highly sensitive to sugar, essential for supporting their energetic way of life. "Hummingbirds need a continuous supply of energy due to their high metabolic rate," an ornithologist notes. "Their capacity to detect and favor sweet nectar is an ideal adaptation to meet their energy requirements."

Remarkably, hummingbirds have adapted their savory taste receptors to sense sweetness, highlighting a unique evolutionary change that emphasizes the crucial role of sugar in their diet. This adaptation enables them to effectively find and ingest the nectar that fuels their swift wing movements and vigorous flying.

The Harsh Reality for Plant-Eaters

Plant-eating animals like cows and horses possess a keen sense of taste, especially when it comes to detecting bitter flavors. This heightened taste sensitivity aids them in steering clear of poisonous plants, which frequently have a bitter flavor. "A zoologist explains that for herbivores, recognizing bitterness is vital for their survival." "It serves as a natural safeguard against ingesting toxic materials."

These animals possess a wide array of taste receptors that enable them to detect slight variations in plant flavors, helping them choose nutritious and safe foods. Their taste buds serve not just for pleasure but as an essential part of their feeding approach.

The Limited Taste Range of Chickens

Unlike other animals, chickens have a rather limited ability to taste. They have approximately 24 taste buds, making them much less sensitive to flavors than many other animals. A poultry scientist notes that chickens depend more on their vision and tactile sense while searching for food. "Their restricted sense of taste aligns with their eating patterns, which prioritize accessibility over flavor."

Even with their few taste buds, chickens are capable of sensing specific flavors like salt and sour, which influence how they feed. Nonetheless, they primarily concentrate on the physical attributes of food, including its texture and size.

To sum up, animals exhibit a diverse and intricate sense of taste, molded by evolutionary forces and their environmental requirements. From the catfish's extensive taste abilities to the dolphins' restricted flavor perception, each species has tailored its taste senses to fit its distinct way of living. Grasping these distinctions enhances our comprehension of animal biology and underscores the remarkable variety of life on Earth.

The vast majority of Earth's oceans remain unexplored, with their depths holding countless mysteries and untold scientific discoveries. While advanced submersibles and sophisticated equipment have helped researchers study deep-sea environments, the high costs of such technology—often running into millions of dollars—have kept ocean exploration largely out of reach for most people. Now, a revolutionary new device called the Maka Niu is changing that paradigm by making deep-sea exploration more accessible and affordable than ever before.

Developed by a team of marine scientists and engineers at the University of Hawaii, the Maka Niu (meaning "coconut eye" in Hawaiian) is a compact, autonomous deep-sea camera system that can descend to depths of up to 2,000 meters—more than five times deeper than the maximum depth reached by trained scuba divers. What makes this device truly revolutionary is its price tag: at just $650 per unit, it costs a fraction of traditional deep-sea exploration equipment.

"The Maka Niu democratizes ocean exploration," says Dr. Jeffrey Drazen, a marine biologist at the University of Hawaii and lead developer of the device. "We wanted to create something that could be used by researchers, citizen scientists, and even high school students to study the deep ocean without breaking the bank."

The device's simple yet effective design consists of a pressure-resistant housing made from standard PVC pipe, off-the-shelf electronics, and a high-definition camera. It can be deployed from any small boat and uses basic weights to sink to predetermined depths. After collecting video footage and environmental data for up to 12 hours, the device automatically releases its weights and floats back to the surface.

Dr. Sarah McTee, an oceanographer at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution who wasn't involved in the project, praises the innovation: "What's particularly exciting about the Maka Niu is how it combines simplicity with functionality. It's essentially democratizing access to the deep sea, which has traditionally been the domain of well-funded research institutions."

The device has already yielded surprising discoveries. During initial tests off the coast of Hawaii, the Maka Niu captured footage of previously undocumented deep-sea creatures and behaviors. "We recorded a rare interaction between two different species of deep-sea fish that had never been observed before," explains Marina Rodriguez, a graduate student involved in the project. "This kind of observation would have been impossible without long-duration deployment at these depths."

But the Maka Niu's potential extends far beyond scientific research. Coastal communities can use it to monitor local marine ecosystems, fishing grounds, and the impacts of climate change. Environmental organizations can deploy it to assess marine protected areas, while educators can use it to give students firsthand exposure to deep-sea environments.

"We're seeing tremendous interest from community groups and schools," says Dr. Craig Smith, a marine ecologist at the University of Hawaii. "The device is simple enough that high school students can assemble it themselves, giving them hands-on experience with both engineering and marine science."

The technology also has practical applications for industries that depend on ocean resources. Small-scale fisheries can use it to survey fish populations, while coastal tourism operators can explore potential diving sites. Even conservation groups are finding innovative uses for the device.

"We're using the Maka Niu to monitor deep-water coral reefs that are threatened by ocean acidification," says Dr. Lisa Chen, a marine conservationist with the Pacific Marine Alliance. "The low cost means we can deploy multiple units simultaneously, giving us a much more comprehensive picture of ecosystem health."

The device's development wasn't without challenges. The team had to overcome significant engineering hurdles to create something both affordable and capable of withstanding extreme pressures at depth. "The biggest challenge was finding the right balance between cost and functionality," explains Dr. Drazen. "We went through numerous iterations before finding a design that worked reliably at depth while remaining within our target price range."

The Maka Niu's success has sparked interest in developing similar low-cost devices for other types of ocean research. The team is currently working on variations that can measure water chemistry, collect biological samples, and even track marine animal movements.

The project has also attracted attention from international organizations interested in expanding ocean research capabilities in developing nations. "Many countries lack the resources for traditional deep-sea research," notes Dr. Maria Santos of the United Nations Ocean Science Program. "The Maka Niu could help bridge this technology gap and enable more inclusive global ocean research."

Looking ahead, the team plans to make the device's designs open-source, allowing others to build and modify their own versions. They're also developing educational materials and training programs to help users make the most of the technology.

"Our goal isn't just to provide access to deep-sea exploration," says Dr. Drazen, "but to build a community of citizen scientists who can contribute to our understanding of the ocean. The more eyes we have studying the deep sea, the better our chances of protecting it."

As climate change and other environmental pressures continue to impact marine ecosystems, tools like the Maka Niu could play a crucial role in monitoring and understanding these changes. By making deep-sea exploration more accessible, this innovative device might just help unlock the mysteries of our oceans' depths—one coconut eye at a time.

The development of the Maka Niu represents a significant step toward democratizing ocean exploration. As Dr. McTee puts it, "Sometimes the most important innovations aren't the most complex or expensive ones, but those that make existing capabilities available to everyone. The Maka Niu does exactly that for deep-sea research."

It’s easy to take your nose for granted—until you can’t use it the way most people do. For individuals born without a sense of smell, a condition known as congenital anosmia, the world is experienced differently. According to new research, that difference goes beyond missing out on aromas; it affects how they breathe, too. A recent study found that people with congenital anosmia sniff less often than those who can smell normally. The findings raise intriguing questions about whether this altered breathing pattern has any impact on overall health.

“Until now, most of us never thought about how the sense of smell might influence the way we inhale,” says Dr. Thomas Hummel, a smell researcher at the Technical University of Dresden Medical School, who was not involved in the study. “This research suggests that smell and breathing are connected more closely than we realized.”

In the study, published in the journal *PLoS ONE*, a team of researchers recruited participants with congenital anosmia—meaning they had never experienced scents—and compared them to a control group of people with fully functioning noses. During the experiment, participants were exposed to scent-related tasks and their breathing patterns were monitored using sensitive equipment.

The results were clear. Individuals with congenital anosmia sniffed less frequently and with less force than their peers. While people with a normal sense of smell often take quick, exploratory sniffs as they navigate their environment—sampling the air for clues about food, danger, or pleasant aromas—those born without smell didn’t show this behavior. “It’s as if the anosmic individuals had little incentive to engage in sniffing because they never get any sensory reward from it,” explains Dr. Maria Larsson, a psychologist at Stockholm University who studies the sense of smell and was not part of the research team.

Breathing through the nose does more than just detect scents. Air passing through the nasal passages is warmed, filtered, and humidified before it reaches the lungs. Specialized cells in the nasal cavity can help protect against pathogens, and the act of sniffing may even play a role in sharpening our attention to the environment. Without the instinctive urge to sniff, could individuals with congenital anosmia be missing out on these subtle benefits?

“That’s one of the big questions,” says Dr. Karyn Rhoads, the study’s lead author and a researcher at the University of Geneva in Switzerland. “We have established that their breathing pattern is different. Now, we want to know if that difference matters.” Could reduced sniffing impact respiratory health, immune function, or even cognitive aspects related to smell, like memory and emotion?

Previous studies have shown that smell has strong ties to emotion and memory. People often recall vivid personal experiences triggered by certain scents, and the lack of smell can alter how individuals relate to food, social interactions, and their own bodies. “Smell isn’t just a ‘bonus’ sense—it’s fundamental to how we perceive and engage with the world,” notes Dr. Larsson.

Still, having congenital anosmia is not necessarily harmful. Many people lead full, healthy lives without ever knowing the scent of roses or fresh bread. The next phase of this research will examine whether reduced sniffing leads to any measurable health differences. For instance, are these individuals more or less prone to nasal infections? Does the absence of smell-driven sniffing change the brain’s response to breathing or influence stress and relaxation?

More work is needed to uncover such connections. Future studies may compare lung function, sleep quality, or the incidence of respiratory conditions between people with congenital anosmia and the general population. Researchers might also investigate whether training or therapies aimed at mimicking normal sniffing patterns could offer any benefits.

For now, the findings serve as a reminder that even the most seemingly automatic behaviors—like breathing—can be influenced by our senses. “We’re learning that smelling and breathing are intertwined in ways we never fully appreciated,” says Dr. Hummel. “This research opens up a new perspective on what it means to live without smell. It’s not just about what they can’t sense; it’s also about how their bodies respond to a scentless world.”

In the end, the study provides a glimpse into the complex interplay between the senses and our basic bodily functions. Understanding these nuances could eventually lead to better support for people with congenital anosmia, ensuring that differences in breathing patterns don’t translate into hidden health disadvantages.

For decades, a tiny, skin-infecting fungus known as Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) has caused catastrophic declines in frog populations worldwide. Regions of Central and South America have borne the brunt, but similar devastation has occurred everywhere from Australia’s Wet Tropics to the Sierra Nevada in California. Species after species fell victim to chytridiomycosis, the lethal disease triggered by Bd. In some places, entire choruses of nighttime callers disappeared.

Now, in certain streams where frogs had nearly vanished, scientists are hearing something unexpected: the familiar croaks and chirps of new generations. Researchers have identified a handful of frog species showing signs of mounting resistance to the fungus. This shift—though still modest—is offering new hope that amphibians are not as defenseless as once believed.

“It’s not a simple comeback story,” says Dr. Karen Lips, an amphibian biologist at the University of Maryland who has studied frog declines for more than 20 years. “We’re not seeing massive rebounds across the board, but we are seeing species that were hit hard now surviving in the presence of Bd. They don’t always thrive as they did before, but they persist.”

One line of evidence comes from field observations in Panama, where the fungus raced through frog communities in the early 2000s. Many species, including the once-common harlequin frogs, went from abundant to scarce in a matter of seasons. But in recent years, researchers have spotted survivors and their offspring clinging on in small but stable populations. According to Dr. Jamie Voyles, a disease ecologist at the University of Nevada, Reno, certain frog species appear to be adapting at the immunological level. “We’ve identified subtle changes in their skin peptides and beneficial skin microbes that may be helping them cope,” she says. “These defenses don’t wipe out the fungus, but they seem to keep it in check.”

The frog’s skin is more than just a barrier—it’s an entire ecosystem. Microbes living on the surface can influence how well Bd takes hold. Some bacteria release antifungal compounds that hinder the pathogen. In places where frogs are rebounding, scientists have found higher proportions of protective microbes. That’s led to experiments in which frogs are treated with probiotic “cocktails” to bolster their skin’s natural defenses. While these attempts are still at an early stage, preliminary results suggest the microbiome approach could complement other conservation tactics.

Another strategy under consideration involves selective breeding. If scientists can identify certain genetic variants that confer resistance, they might create lineages of frogs better equipped to survive with Bd in the wild. But Dr. Lips cautions that these interventions have to be done carefully. “We’re talking about complex ecosystems, not just frogs in isolation,” she says. “If we release a frog population that hasn’t interacted with its native parasites, predators, or competitors for years, we could disrupt the local balance. We have to think holistically.”

In parallel, some researchers are testing targeted antifungals in controlled environments. Amphibians are collected from disease hotspots, treated in laboratories or field stations, then re-released. This is no small feat. “Handling wild frogs repeatedly is stressful to them—and us,” says Dr. Roberto Ibáñez, a scientific coordinator at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute in Panama, who has been involved in some of these projects. “Still, without trying these approaches, we can’t learn what works.”

The global scale of Bd’s impact means that solutions won’t be one-size-fits-all. The fungus thrives in cool, moist conditions—hence its success in mountain cloud forests—and different frog species have different vulnerabilities. Some species, like the mountain yellow-legged frog in California, have shown that, over time, populations can develop higher survival rates even in infected habitats. Others remain perilously close to extinction.

At the same time, there’s mounting interest in understanding why some regions have been less affected. For instance, in certain parts of Asia where Bd is present, it hasn’t caused widespread die-offs. Studying these “tolerance hotspots” could provide clues. Scientists wonder if local amphibians have coexisted with the fungus for so long that a stable equilibrium developed.

Underlying all these efforts is the realization that amphibian declines—once widely viewed as unstoppable—may at least be mitigated. “A decade ago, I would’ve told you that Bd was an absolute death sentence for many species,” says Dr. Voyles. “Now, we’re seeing that some populations are evolving. It’s slow, it’s partial, but it’s real.”

Conservation groups, including the Panama Amphibian Rescue and Conservation Project and the Amphibian Survival Alliance, are banking on these findings to inform their next moves. They’ve begun to tailor their interventions based on local species’ responses, whether that means focusing on genetic screening, tweaking probiotic formulations, or coordinating habitat restoration to improve frogs’ baseline health. Healthy frogs, after all, are better positioned to resist infection.

No one is declaring victory. The world’s amphibians still face habitat loss, pollution, climate change, and invasive predators. But Bd, once seemingly an unbeatable enemy, may not remain unchallenged forever. “What’s unfolding now,” says Dr. Lips, “is a kind of evolutionary arms race. The fungus doesn’t vanish, but neither do the frogs. They’re finding ways to coexist, and that’s something we couldn’t have imagined 20 years ago.”

For conservationists, even modest signs of resistance are cause for cautious optimism. Amid the relentless tide of wildlife declines, the idea that frogs can learn new survival tricks suggests that with the right help, nature can adapt. It’s a tough lesson—earned through painstaking fieldwork and countless hours of lab experiments—but it points toward a future where frogs and fungus share the forest floor without one side disappearing entirely.

Keurig Dr Pepper has agreed to pay a civil penalty to settle U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission charges over claims made by the beverage company that its single-serve pods, or K-Cups, could be "effectively" recycled.

The statements were misleading, the SEC said. Keurig Dr Pepper neither denied nor admitted the regulator's findings in the $1.5 million settlement agreement.

The SEC said Keurig Dr Pepper wrote in annual reports in 2019 and 2020 its K-Cup pods could be "effectively" recycled, but didn't mention that two of the largest recycling companies in the U.S. expressed concerns about that and said they didn't intend to recycle the pods.

The omission violated the Securities Exchange Act, which requires companies to make accurate disclosures, the regulator said.

Keurig Dr Pepper changed the type of plastic used in the K-Cup pods in 2020, saying that made them easier to recycle. However, many recycling facilities still don't accept the new packaging , which is made of polypropylene plastic.

A spokesperson said the company encourages consumers to check with their local recycling facilities about the pods, "as they are not recycled in many communities."

Keurig Dr Pepper announced plans to launch compostable pods earlier this year. "We remain committed to a better, more standardized U.S. recycling system," the spokesperson added.

K-Cup sales made up a significant portion of the company's coffee sales in 2019 and 2020, and internal company research showed environmental concerns about pod disposal were a significant factor for consumers thinking about buying Keurig machines, according to the SEC.

"A lot of recycling companies are actually faced with issues of 'wishful-cycling,' as it's called," said Yuliya Strizhakova, an associate professor of marketing at Rutgers School of Business-Camden who has studied single-serve beverage pods. "Consumers tend to recycle more things, and they hope they can be recycled…when in fact, they cannot, for various reasons."

The settlement comes as regulators take a hard look at green claims made by companies. The European Commission recently sent warning letters to 20 airlines about overstating the use of low-carbon fuels. In the U.S., the Federal Trade Commission, which regulates advertising, in coming months is expected to release updated guidelines for marketers regarding green claims. The SEC has proposed a rule requiring companies to disclose greenhouse gas emissions, though the rollout has been paused pending legal challenges.

"On the positive side, it's good to see that they're following through," said Frank Maguire, vice president at the advertising exchange Sharethrough, of recent regulatory actions. "On the other side, I think brands and major companies are still hesitant to talk about sustainability efforts for a number of reasons, one of which is just the fear of being called out for saying the wrong thing."

As part of the settlement, Keurig Dr Pepper also agreed to a cease-and-desist order, according to the SEC, meaning the company will abide by the law when publishing annual reports.

"Hopefully the big takeaway is for other companies to be much more careful with using recyclable claims or green claims, and be more accountable for what they claim," Strizhakova said.

Before 19-year-old Davontez Johnson found himself in a preschool classroom at Dorothy I. Heights Elementary, he was a senior at a nearby high school who, like many students his age, was unsure of what he wanted to do with his life. Not in his wildest dreams could he have imagined himself standing on a colorful carpet, leading a gaggle of 4-year-olds in a chant and dance about phonics.

“Words have parts — that’s syl-a-bles,” he said, enunciating for effect. The preschoolers craned their heads up at Johnson and echoed him. “Clap your hands now, syl-a-bles! Stomp your feet now, syl-a-bles!”

Johnson is part of the Leading Men Fellowship, which trains young Black and Latino men to become early literacy instructors in preschool classrooms across the country. It’s a program that aims to tackle several problems at once: a shortage of early educators, a dearth of Black and Latino male teachers and the acute challenges boys of color face in schools because of their race and gender.

“We’re not only affecting change in the classroom with these school students, but (we’re) also developing these young future educators,” said Ivan Douglas of the Literacy Lab, which runs the Leading Men Fellowship.

Many fellows, like Johnson, are recruited right out of high school. After an interview process and intensive summer training, they go to work in schools where they may be among the only male educators. Fellows make between $16.50 and $18 an hour.

A former high school offensive lineman, Johnson knows some parents would say he looks out of place in a preschool classroom. And the statistics back him up: Less than 1% of elementary and early education public school teachers are Black men, according to federal data. But that’s part of the reason he wanted to do it.

“I really thought it was a great opportunity. Because I know if I saw someone like me, you know, in pre-K, I’d be pretty excited,” Johnson said. “You don’t see a lot of young Black males.”

Researchers have shown that Black male students encounter discrimination before they even set foot in a kindergarten classroom, facing higher rates of expulsion and suspension from preschool even though evidence suggests they do not misbehave more than their white peers. Boys also are far more likely than girls to be expelled.

But there’s a growing body of evidence that Black teachers can make a difference for Black students — and for Black boys in particular. In the years since the Leading Men Fellowship was founded, in 2016, researchers have repeatedly found that students of color seem to fare better when they have teachers who look like them.

Johns Hopkins University economist Nicholas Papageorge, who is based not far from Heights Elementary, studies the impact of Black teachers on Black students. His research found that Black teachers have higher expectations for Black students than do non-Black teachers.

“If a Black student had a white teacher and a Black teacher, that white teacher had systematically lower expectations,” Papageorge said.

His later research found Black students who have a Black teacher are less likely to drop out of high school and more likely to attend college. The effect of having a Black teacher had the greatest impact on Black boys from low-income households.

Through his coursework, Johnson has learned the intricacies of early education — and that it involves a surprising amount of singing and dancing for someone not working on Broadway. Children learn best by repetition, and when they can pair information with movements and song.

Bridget Jeffrys, whose preschool classroom hosts Johnson, said she had never worked alongside a male educator until Johnson arrived at the start of the last school year. She said she’s watched Johnson grow more confident with her students, going from reserved to enthusiastic. Jeffrys said his voice and dance moves could use some work, but he performs the songs with such heart that it doesn’t matter.

“It was so beautiful because usually you don’t see men really get down to the child level,” Jeffrys said. “That excited them even more. A lot of kids think he’s a big kid.”

Along with teaching at Heights Elementary, Johnson is studying political science at University of Maryland Global Campus and hopes to go into politics. His colleagues, though, are encouraging him to stick with teaching.

While Johnson is there to provide targeted literacy instruction, he has been fully integrated into the school day. His second week in the classroom, he sang the class’s morning greeting song in a robot voice. When a child is squirming on the carpet or wandering away from story time, Johnson is there to rein them in.

On this October day, Johnson pulled students aside to help them work on writing their names. He had only been with this cohort for a couple weeks, but many students were drawn to him. During free-play time, he encouraged a student who was working on a crayon rubbing of a leaf.

“You’ve done a wonderful job,” he said to the girl, who stared up at him, eager for reassurance. Another student interrupted him by handing him a fistful of play money.

After lunchtime, as most of the preschoolers sat on the carpet held rapt by a story read by Jeffrys, 4-year-old Kodi Hendricks wandered toward the door and peered into the hallway until Johnson beckoned him back. Johnson bent his large frame to tie the boy’s shoe and then they sat together for a penmanship lesson.

“What’s the first letter?” he asked the boy.

“K,” he replied. Johnson showed him, in slow motion, how to draw a K.

“No, I can’t do it,” said the boy.

“It’s all right,” Johnson said. He urged him on.

“You can do it. It just takes practice.”

TikTok faces lawsuits from more than a dozen U.S. states that allege the popular video platform, which has attracted attention for the sometimes risky challenges it hosts, has helped put young people in danger and harmed their mental health.

A bipartisan coalition of 14 attorneys general on Tuesday announced the filing of legal actions against TikTok in their own state courts.

“TikTok claims that their platform is safe for young people, but that is far from true,” said New York Attorney General Letitia James, who leads the coalition along with California Attorney General Rob Bonta.

“In New York and across the country, young people have died or gotten injured doing dangerous TikTok challenges and many more are feeling more sad, anxious and depressed because of TikTok’s addictive features,” James said.

TikTok says it strongly disagrees with the claims and believes many of them are inaccurate and misleading. The company said it provides robust safeguards and has voluntarily launched features such as screen-time limits and privacy by default for users under age 16.

TikTok has amassed an audience of tens of millions of users, including many children and young people, by serving up catchy short videos using a secretive algorithm that seems to tap viewers’ deepest desires. But critics have slammed the app’s allegedly addictive aspects and its hosting of trendy challenges that have enticed users, particularly young people, to engage in antisocial or dangerous behavior.

James noted that a 15-year-old Manhattan boy who died in 2023 while subway surfing—riding on the outside of a subway car—allegedly had subway surfing videos in his TikTok account. The attorney general also pointed to the so-called Kia Challenge, a TikTok trend where a number of videos showed users how to steal certain Kia and Hyundai models.

TikTok is accused of violating New York law against false advertising by claiming that the app is safe for young users and by failing to disclose its adverse health consequences. The company is also accused of negligence and for violating product liability law.

New York has asked a Manhattan judge to order TikTok to turn over profits from ads directed at teens and preteen users in the state, and to pay punitive damages. The state cited a Harvard University study showing that TikTok in 2022 generated $2 billion from U.S.-based users aged 13 to 17.

The coalition filing the lawsuits is made up of attorneys general for several other jurisdictions: Illinois, Kentucky, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Mississippi, New Jersey, North Carolina, Oregon, South Carolina, Vermont, Washington and the District of Columbia.

The attorneys general chose to file the lawsuits in their own courts rather than as a single action in federal court, which could complicate TikTok’s efforts to defend against the allegations.

So far, 23 attorneys general have filed actions against TikTok over its conduct toward youth, according to California’s Bonta. These include existing actions under way from attorneys general for Utah, Nevada, Indiana, New Hampshire, Nebraska, Arkansas, Iowa, Kansas and Texas.

President Biden in April signed bipartisan legislation that would force TikTok, which is owned by Beijing-based ByteDance, to sever ties with China if it wants to keep operating in the U.S.

TikTok has challenged that legislation in court, citing free speech arguments, but in September faced skepticism from appeals court judges. The intelligence community has warned that China might be able to exploit the app, which has about 170 million U.S. users.

The lightning rod. Bifocals. Swim fins. Benjamin Franklin is known for pioneering new solutions for common problems. 

A new analysis of Early American paper money shows he also played a vital role in thwarting counterfeiters.  

Franklin, who was a printer, among his other roles, was known for marking his early paper money with images of intricately veined leaves that were nearly impossible for counterfeiters to copy, using a variety of fonts, some available only to him, and intentionally lacing the text with misspellings. 

But scientists say Franklin took things a step further to stave off fraudsters. Other distinguishing characteristics of Franklin’s money—the new research revealed through advanced atomic-level imaging methods—were more subtle. He used a unique black ink. His paper glimmered. Blue threads decorated the surface, and finer fibers were woven throughout.  

Researchers detailed the innovations in a paper published Monday in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The findings describe previously unknown methods Franklin developed to safeguard printed money notes against counterfeiting. 

Khachatur Manukyan, research associate professor of physics and astronomy at the University of Notre Dame, led a team that analyzed nearly 600 paper money notes printed in America from 1709 to 1790. The trove belongs to the Rare Books and Special Collections of the Hesburgh Library at Notre Dame and includes legitimate bills produced by Franklin and other Colonial printers as well as fakes manufactured by counterfeiters.  

Franklin and his associates held lucrative government contracts to print the paper currencies of the Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Delaware colonies. Later, after Franklin retired, his associates carried on with the novel techniques leading up to the Revolutionary War, when the Continental Congress ordered the first national currency to finance the American Revolution. Their bills bore their names—“B. Franklin” or “Hall and Sellers,” for example, identifying Franklin, his former business partner David Hall, and Hall’s subsequent partner, William Sellers. 

The type of analysis Manukyan’s team conducted is common in physics and chemistry, he said, but is new for conservation science. 

The researchers took samples from the paper money and examined them in increasingly fine detail using a variety of microscopes, including a high-resolution model that passed beams of electrons through the samples to produce images of the atomic details. 

“We take a very, very tiny piece of money,” Manukyan said. “It is a thousand times tinier than a human hair. We can image even single atoms.” 

Researchers discovered the black ink used by Franklin and his associates was made of graphite. The blue threads in their bills were dyed with indigo, a plant-based pigment. Their paper was strengthened with muscovite, a variety of mica. 

Combined, the features created bills that were more durable and of a higher quality, Manukyan said. 

“He has small muscovite inside the paper early on,” Manukyan said. “Then we see it appear on the surface and glimmer. No others had this among those we analyzed. Indigo colored threads were unique to Benjamin Franklin’s money. The black pigment is a more vivid black than the others.” 

Bills produced by other printers included in the analysis used lamp black or bone black ink; Prussian blue, a mineral-based pigment; and a more common type of paper strengthened with kaolinite, a clay mineral.  

While it is difficult to know to what extent counterfeiting occurred, it is evident that it was a concern. Some bills bore the warning “To counterfeit is Death,” a reminder that making funny money was a capital offense. And Franklin, John Adams and others expressed concern that the British government was circulating fake bills to undermine the colonial economy and rebellion.  

Amid those concerns, the Continental Congress recalled more than 41 million Continental dollars, swapping new bills for two lots of compromised notes. 

There were 11 emissions, or printings, from 1775 to 1779, according to Farley Grubb, an economics professor at the University of Delaware and author of “The Continental Dollar.” “Two were clearly counterfeited.”  

While phony bills might have been difficult for a regular person to spot—depending on the quality of the fake—the authenticity of cash could be tested with a counterfeit detector sheet.  

“The original printer would print the exact same notes from the same plate on a blue paper,” said Joseph E. Boling, vice president of the American Numismatic Association. 

“Those notes weren’t numbered, and they were not signed. With the detector sheet in hand, [merchants] could compare it” with circulating bills, he said.   

Today, modern currency incorporates safeguards that are reminiscent of the techniques Franklin pioneered. 

The hundred-dollar bill, which bears Franklin’s portrait, is protected by a 3-D blue security ribbon that is woven into the note. A pink security thread is concealed in the fiber. Color-shifting numerals change from copper to green. A hologram of the Liberty Bell and a faint watermark tattoo the paper.  

Even so, people still try to get away with passing fakes.  

Since October, according to the Secret Service, counterfeiters have passed fake Benjamins worth more than $52 million—the largest total value of any counterfeited U.S. bill today.

As Floridians emerge from Hurricane Milton, they are finding unexpected visitors in flooded streets, backyards or even their homes: displaced wild animals.  

An alligator was caught on video Thursday morning resting on the porch of a home in Tampa.  

Another lunged at the tire of a vehicle driving through floodwaters in North Fort Myers during the storm Wednesday night, according toa local news report.  

Wildlife experts warn people to leave the animals alone. 

“Alligators really want nothing to do with us,” said Chris Gillette, a wildlife rehabilitator and co-owner of Bellowing Acres, an animal-rescue facility in northern Florida. “But don’t go into alligator habitat, which is anywhere that has become flooded, especially if you can’t see.” 

Florida’s semitropical climate is home to a variety of unusual wildlife, including 700 species of land animals, more than 200 species of freshwater fish, and thousands of terrestrial insects and other invertebrates, according to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission. 

Wild mammals, snakes pushed out of their burrows, and insects might seek shelter in suburban backyards, according to Frank Mazzotti, associate professor of wildlife ecology at the University of Florida. 

“Animals that like to keep their feet dry go to high ground, and that’s why people report seeing concentrations of snakes,” Mazzotti said.  

The state is also home to an estimated 1.3 million alligators, although not all live in areas affected by Hurricane Milton, which crossed central Florida Wednesday night and early Thursday.  

Like many animals, alligators can sense the drop in barometric pressure before a storm arrives.  

“They’re just going to sink under the water, hold their breath for six hours and just sit there,” said Gillette, who tends to half a dozen alligators that were deemed a nuisance and brought to him by professional trappers.  

When the storm clears, alligators begin to move again, and flooding allows them to move freely through places that would usually be obstructed by fences or land, Gillette said. “You definitely have to be aware.” 

Alligators aren’t hunting for food during a storm and don’t need to eat as frequently as other animals, said Savannah Boan, a park director at Gatorland wildlife park in Orlando. “In the wild they will eat maybe 10 or 15 times a year and be fine,” she said. None of Gatorland’s alligators and crocodiles have escaped in the park’s 75 years, Boan said. 

Like many wild animals, alligators will bite if they feel threatened, but aren’t looking to eat people, according to all three wildlife experts. Between 1946 and 2022, there have been 26 human fatalities from alligator bites, according to Florida state figures. Two people were killed by alligators in Florida in 2023, according to news reports. 

In 2017, Mazzotti and colleagues attached radio collars to eight alligators in Everglades National Park to track their movements. When Hurricane Irma came through that September, the researchers found the alligators didn’t seem very bothered. Most stayed close to their normal hunting grounds. 

“Some animals tried to hide out, and some animals just were like nothing was happening,” Mazzotti said. “We didn’t notice a high degree of mortality or really any bad effects to the alligators.”

In a significant development for both consumers and environmental advocates, Keurig Dr Pepper has agreed to pay a $1.5 million penalty following charges by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) for making misleading claims about the recyclability of its K-Cup coffee pods. A coalition of state attorneys general filed lawsuits against TikTok on Wednesday, alleging that the social media platform deliberately employs addictive features and promotes dangerous challenges that put young users at risk of physical and mental harm.

The lawsuits, filed by attorneys general from eight states including California, Florida, and New York, claim that TikTok's algorithm intentionally serves up harmful content to teenagers and children while downplaying the platform's risks to parents.

"TikTok has become a digital playground where our children are the unwitting test subjects in a dangerous social experiment," said California Attorney General Rob Bonta. "The company's aggressive data collection practices and manipulative algorithms are designed to keep young users scrolling endlessly, regardless of the consequences to their well-being."

At the center of the legal challenge are TikTok's viral challenges, which often encourage users to perform risky stunts or dangerous activities. The lawsuit cites several notorious examples, including the "blackout challenge," which allegedly led to multiple deaths among young users who attempted to choke themselves until losing consciousness.

Dr. Sarah Thompson, a child psychiatrist specializing in digital media's impact on youth development, explains, "These challenges exploit adolescents' natural desire for peer approval and recognition. When combined with TikTok's highly effective algorithm, it creates a perfect storm for risky behavior."

The lawsuits also target TikTok's addictive features, such as the infinite scroll and personalized "For You" page. According to the legal filings, these features are specifically designed to maximize user engagement, particularly among young people who are more susceptible to addictive behaviors.

"Our investigation revealed that TikTok knows exactly what it's doing," said Florida Attorney General Ashley Moody. "Internal documents show the company deliberately engineered its platform to exploit young users' vulnerability to persuasive technology."

TikTok, owned by Chinese company ByteDance, defended its practices in a statement: "We have industry-leading safeguards for teenagers, including default private accounts and screen time limits. We are committed to protecting our community while preserving creative expression on our platform."
