NASA has initiated a bold mission to study Europa, Jupiter's mysterious moon, by launching a spacecraft aimed at determining if this frozen world could support life. The spacecraft, launched on Monday, seeks to explore the enigmatic ocean beneath Europa's icy surface, offering an exciting opportunity for scientists investigating the possibility of life beyond Earth.

Europa, among Jupiter's 79 moons, has captivated researchers for years because of its frozen exterior and the potential existence of an ocean beneath it. This mission, which is a component of NASA's larger initiative to investigate the outer solar system, aims to assess if Europa's ocean could sustain life similar to that on Earth. "Europa is considered one of the top locations in our solar system for seeking evidence of life," stated Pranay Mishra, a planetary scientist participating in the mission. "The ocean hidden beneath its thick ice layer could potentially harbor conditions suitable for life."

Outfitted with a range of scientific tools, the spacecraft will perform an in-depth examination of Europa's icy exterior and the ocean beneath it. The spacecraft will study the moon's makeup, geological features, and possible ability to support life. "We're searching for the fundamental components necessary for life," explained Jim Free, NASA's Associate Administrator for the Exploration Systems Development Mission Directorate. "This mission aims to determine if Europa possesses the essential elements for life to develop."

A key goal of the mission is to evaluate how thick Europa's ice layer is and how deep its ocean extends. Researchers think that the ocean, heated by tidal forces from Jupiter's strong gravitational pull, might interact with the moon's rocky mantle, possibly forming a livable environment. "The interaction between the ocean and the rocky seabed might supply the chemical energy essential for sustaining life," stated Laurie Leshin, a prominent astrobiologist.

The spacecraft will additionally look for water vapor plumes that could be emerging from Europa's surface. If verified, these plumes might provide insight into the ocean's makeup without needing to penetrate the ice. "Identifying and studying these plumes could revolutionize our understanding," remarked Gina DiBraccio, a project scientist involved in the mission. "It would enable us to analyze Europa's ocean indirectly and search for indications of life."

This mission to Europa is a component of a larger initiative to investigate the outer solar system and assess the possibility of life existing beyond our planet. Despite the valuable insights gained from NASA's earlier missions to Jupiter and its moons, Europa continues to be one of the most fascinating subjects of study. "Europa is a realm full of marvels," Mishra commented. "The possibility that it could support life makes it a top exploration target."

The spacecraft will take several years to reach Europa, during which it will conduct multiple flybys to collect data and adjust its course. Upon reaching Europa, the spacecraft will circle the moon and carry out comprehensive surveys, transmitting data back to Earth for scientists to analyze. "This mission exemplifies human curiosity and our drive to investigate the unknown," stated Free. "We are close to finding out if Europa might serve as another habitat for life within our solar system."

As the spacecraft sets off on its mission, both scientists and space enthusiasts are excitedly awaiting the findings it will reveal. "The quest to discover life outside of Earth is among the most significant inquiries we can pursue," stated Leshin. "This mission moves us nearer to finding an answer." The mission, with its ability to unveil the mysteries of Europa's ocean, marks a major advancement in our pursuit to comprehend the universe and our role in it.

In an age where social media drives many of our decisions, new research suggests that the more photos we share of a destination, the less appealing it becomes to others planning their special events. This phenomenon, dubbed "social media saturation effect" by researchers, reveals how our desire for uniqueness influences our venue choices.

A study published in the Journal of Consumer Psychology found that when people see multiple social media posts of a location, they're significantly less likely to choose it for their own meaningful events, such as weddings, engagement photos, or milestone celebrations.

"People want their special moments to feel distinctive and personal," explains Dr. Sarah Chen, lead researcher at Cornell University's Department of Consumer Behavior. "When they see a location repeatedly on Instagram or Facebook, it loses its perceived uniqueness, regardless of how objectively beautiful or suitable it might be."

The research team analyzed the behavior of 2,500 couples planning their wedding venues and found that locations frequently featured on social media platforms experienced a 35% decrease in booking inquiries compared to equally attractive but less publicized venues.

James Morrison, a wedding photographer with 15 years of experience, has observed this trend firsthand. "I've seen stunning venues lose their appeal simply because they became too 'Instagrammable,'" he says. "Couples nowadays often specifically request locations that haven't been 'done to death' on social media."

The impact extends beyond wedding venues. Popular tourist destinations are experiencing what tourism experts call "social media fatigue." Mark Thompson, director of the International Tourism Management Institute, notes, "We're seeing a growing number of travelers actively avoiding places that dominate their social media feeds, opting instead for less photographed alternatives."

This behavior reflects a broader psychological phenomenon known as "uniqueness seeking," according to Dr. Rachel Williams, a social psychologist at Stanford University. "Humans have an inherent need to feel special and different," she explains. "When we see something become too common or accessible on social media, it threatens our ability to use that thing or place as a marker of uniqueness."

The study also revealed an interesting paradox: while people avoid over-exposed locations for their own special events, they continue to contribute to the problem by sharing their own photos, potentially diminishing the appeal for others.

Some venues are responding to this trend by implementing "photo-free zones" or offering exclusive access times for photography. The Historic Bellview Estate in Vermont, for example, now limits social media photography to specific areas, helping maintain the venue's perceived uniqueness.

"We've seen a 40% increase in bookings since implementing these policies," says Estate manager Patricia Collins. "Couples appreciate knowing their venue won't be all over social media by the time their event happens."

For those planning special events, experts recommend:
- Exploring venues that limit social media exposure
- Considering less-photographed locations
- Looking for unique angles or perspectives of popular venues
- Focusing on personal meaning rather than social media appeal

The research suggests a broader shift in consumer behavior, where oversaturation on social media can actually decrease a location's desirability. "It's a reminder that in our highly connected world, sometimes less exposure is more valuable," concludes Dr. Chen.

As social media continues to influence our choices, this research highlights an important consideration for both consumers and businesses: in a world where everything is shared, uniqueness becomes an increasingly valuable commodity.

A San Francisco startup aiming to help dogs live longer, healthier lives has just raised $45 million in funding, highlighting a growing interest among venture-capital firms in longevity technologies—this time, not just for humans. The company, named Loyal, is developing drugs intended to slow the effects of aging in dogs and, if successful, could open the door to new approaches in age-related care for pets.

“We love our dogs like family members,” says Celine Halioua, Loyal’s founder and CEO, “but they simply don’t live as long as we want them to. At Loyal, we’re trying to address the underlying biology of aging so that our pets can enjoy more happy and active years with us.”

Founded in 2019, Loyal has drawn attention from high-profile investors as the pet industry continues to expand. According to the American Pet Products Association, Americans spend more than $100 billion a year on their pets, reflecting a strong appetite for products and services that improve animal health and longevity. With this latest round of funding, Loyal plans to continue its research, run clinical trials, and prepare the groundwork for bringing its first products to market.

The startup’s core idea is to develop pharmaceuticals that target the biological mechanisms of aging. Instead of addressing one disease at a time—such as arthritis or heart conditions—Loyal hopes to treat aging itself as a risk factor for multiple diseases. If successful, the drugs could extend not only the length of dogs’ lives, but also the quality of those extra years.

Dr. Matt Kaeberlein, a longevity researcher at the University of Washington who is not affiliated with Loyal, notes that the concept of treating aging as a medical condition is gaining traction in the scientific community. “The past decade has shown us that aging is modifiable,” he says. “If we can slow down the aging process, we may be able to significantly reduce the incidence of age-related diseases. Doing this for dogs is an appealing and achievable first step, given their relatively short lifespans and the strength of owner interest.”

Venture-capital investors have been paying close attention. While several longevity startups focus on human aging, the pet market offers a unique entry point. Dogs have shorter lifespans than people, meaning that clinical trials can yield data more quickly. The pet health market is also less strictly regulated than human pharmaceuticals, potentially speeding up the time it takes for a product to reach consumers. “Investors see an opportunity to generate returns while contributing to a growing field with vast potential,” says Mark Davies, a biotech investment analyst.

Loyal’s funding round places it among a cohort of longevity-focused startups that have recently raised significant capital. These companies aim to tap into a future where therapies could prevent or slow degenerative conditions across species. Some industry watchers believe that if these therapies are successful in dogs, the lessons learned could guide similar approaches for human medicine. “There’s a lot we can learn about aging from animal models,” Dr. Kaeberlein explains. “Dogs share our environment and many of our health risks, making them an ideal species to study.”

Still, the journey from concept to commercialization is long. Drug development is fraught with uncertainty, clinical trials can take years, and not every promising idea leads to a safe and effective product. Loyal must navigate a complex web of scientific, regulatory, and market challenges. “It’s one thing to prove something works in a laboratory setting,” says Davies, “and another to demonstrate safety, efficacy, and reliability at scale.”

For now, Loyal’s investors remain optimistic. The funding round, led by prominent venture firms, suggests that even with the known challenges, the company’s approach resonates with those holding the purse strings. “We look for investments that can reshape markets,” says an unnamed investor involved in the deal. “If Loyal’s approach pans out, it could fundamentally change how we think about pet health and aging.”

In the meantime, pet owners eagerly follow these developments. While it may be several years before a longevity treatment hits store shelves or veterinarians’ offices, the idea that science could help extend the time we spend with our furry friends is appealing. “Dogs bring us so much joy,” says Halioua. “Why not give them the healthiest, longest lives we can?”

As research continues, Loyal’s latest funding round signals a broader shift in how we view aging—not just as an inevitable decline, but as a biological process we might someday influence. For dogs, and perhaps one day for humans, that shift could mean more vibrant years together.

When an image popped up on a Reddit thread dedicated to obscure pop-culture sightings, most users scrolled right past. It showed a dimly lit backstage corridor, six people standing shoulder-to-shoulder. The first five were easily recognizable names—movie stars, a television host, a chart-topping singer, a stand-up comedian, and a retired basketball legend. The sixth person, lurking a step behind the others, wore a baseball cap, glasses, and a guarded half-smile. Labelled only as “celebrity number six,” that individual’s identity became the subject of an unexpectedly intense online hunt.

This collective effort, which started on a Tuesday evening in early September and lasted nearly a month, pulled in thousands of participants from Twitter, TikTok, and multiple private Discord servers. Some people ran image searches through digitized yearbooks, while others flipped through scanned copies of entertainment magazines from the early ’90s. A few enlisted help from autograph collectors who specialize in Hollywood’s lesser-known figures. Others reached out directly to production staff of old variety specials, since the photo’s original source was rumored to be a behind-the-scenes snapshot from a forgotten TV benefit aired on a local Los Angeles station decades ago.

“At first, I joined in just because I had ten spare minutes,” said Nina Coleman, a 32-year-old set decorator in Atlanta who posted side-by-side facial comparisons of potential matches. “Then I got hooked. The more I dug, the more I realized how much I rely on other people’s expertise. One person would identify the hallway as belonging to a certain studio, someone else would recall that studio was used for a 1993 charity telethon, and next thing you know, we had a solid lead.”

Participants who spend their weekends identifying obscure band members in music videos or comparing still frames from old VHS recordings have done this sort of thing before, but rarely with such a varied team. The crowd included a New York-based casting assistant, a Chicago archivist who specializes in early cable broadcasts, and a group of Los Angeles film students with a knack for freeze-framing out-of-print documentaries. The search gradually took on the feel of a community project, with volunteers maintaining a shared spreadsheet that listed every guess—more than 400 names at one point—and noted why each was ruled out.

“All these tactics illustrate the power of crowdsourcing,” said David Sternberg, a media historian at UCLA who followed the effort from the sidelines. “When you get enough people contributing their niche knowledge, you fill in gaps that any single researcher would struggle to cover. It’s a form of puzzle-solving that’s unique to our digital age. You can have a hobbyist in Kansas matching a wallpaper pattern to a known green room, and a Hollywood lighting technician confirming the era based on the type of Fresnel lamps visible in the background.”

The turning point came when a user who goes by “MaraKnows” recalled seeing a similar event while cataloging old press photos for a private collector. They remembered a minor television actor who frequently appeared at charity events but never scored major film roles. That memory prompted a flurry of posts, and after more cross-checking with talent rosters from a 1993 earthquake relief broadcast, one name kept resurfacing: Gary Thurman, a stand-in and occasional warm-up comic who worked behind the scenes on numerous Los Angeles-based productions.

Initially, nobody could find official credits for Thurman beyond a few fleeting mentions in trade publications. Eventually, a longtime union publicist stepped in. The publicist confirmed that Thurman had indeed volunteered at an event in Burbank in early 1994. A staff photo from that event, found in a digital archive hosted by the Los Angeles Public Library, matched the posture, cap, and glasses of the mystery figure. After careful verification, the community concluded that “celebrity number six” was actually just a well-liked bit player in Hollywood’s busy ecosystem—someone known mainly to crew members and local comics, not the household name many expected.

Reactions ranged from amused disappointment to genuine satisfaction. “I’d never heard of Gary Thurman before,” said DeAndre Miller, a documentary editor who hopped into the search after seeing a TikTok snippet about it. “But I guess that’s the point. Sometimes, the solution isn’t a huge star. Sometimes it’s a guy who quietly helped make other people look good.”

As users updated the Reddit thread’s title to reflect the discovery, most agreed that the process, rather than the outcome, was what really mattered. “We showed that no single database or recognition app can beat a crowd of curious humans,” said Coleman. “It took a whole bunch of us, comparing notes, making odd guesses, checking obscure sources. Honestly, that’s the best part.”

When David Lane first started teaching, one of his students called him "Humpty Dumpty." That was enough for the high-school art instructor in Rochester, N.Y., to swap his low-slung pants, held up with suspenders, for ones that hit higher. Though it felt like a small adjustment, Lane found the altered shape a big confidence booster. "It lengthens your legs," said the 45-year-old, who stands at 5'10. "It makes me feel taller."

He didn't yet know it, but Lane was embracing the "rule of thirds," a Hollywood styling trick that dictates that a man's shirt or sweater should cover the upper third of his body, and his pants fill out the lower two. The goal: to mimic the classic proportions of old-school movie-star garb—think Cary Grant's tailored slacks from the '50s that, with their higher-rise, fastened neatly around the navel. "It looks sharp," said British designer Charlie Casely-Hayford, noting that no matter one's body type, the technique helps "balance it out."

Casely-Hayford considers the "rule of thirds" to be a cousin to art's "Golden Ratio," which holds that in a painting, visual harmony is achieved when smaller sections are in specific proportion to larger ones—much like the sections of an outfit. "It applies some of that traditional compositional thinking" to a look, he explained. Still, you needn't be a wonk to work out how high to hoist your pants: "It's generally the natural waist point, around the belly button," he said.

This idea might be based on age-old geometry, but it has modern fans. Celebrities like Donald Glover, Paul Mescal and Harry Styles now play by the rule in higher-waisted trousers with tucked tops. The style hack has also gone viral: TikTok videos tagged with "rule of thirds" have been viewed more than five million times.

But though the technique is trendy, it's not exactly easy. "You have to know your proportions," explained London stylist Eric Down, who works with stars like Chris Hemsworth and Henry Cavill. Added Sean Dixon, the co-founder of Savile Row tailor Richard James, "There's a definite balance to be struck, depending on the individual figure."

That's especially true for men with rounder builds. Casely-Hayford noted that clients with "a slight paunch" should find pants that hit just above the belly button. "Nearly every time, that really flatters their shape."

"If your pants hit at the widest point of your stomach, they can draw attention to that," said Down. For huskier bodies, he recommends pairing such pants with a jacket or button-up that falls a little lower, just above the hip, which "draws the eye down."

Bryan O'Sullivan, 42, an interior designer based in London and New York, said that along with "pulling in the tummy," the technique helps his backside seem more toned, especially with darker denim or crisp khaki, which drapes nicely across the curve of the lower torso. "It gives you a good bum," he said.

For best results, consider slacks with straight, slightly wider legs . "Pants tend to fall cleaner when they're cut straight," said Peter Zottolo, 48, a photographer from San Francisco, who recommends khakis from J.Crew and denim from Ben Davis. Stylist Down said pants in thicker fabrics, such as the trousers by British designer Nigel Cabourn, "fall better with a bit of weight." Skinny belts help add some subtle definition between the waist and chest.

As for tops, consider shorter, even boxier shapes . Buck Mason and Lady White Co. make shirts with slightly abbreviated hems. An unexpected jacket can also make the proportions more modern. O'Sullivan layers a cropped, colorful Bode jacket over a tightly tucked white tee and wide-leg trousers, "which gives it a spin."

He also adds rubber clogs, like those from Simone Rocha, for a contemporary edge. Even though the silhouette riffs on old movies, O'Sullivan said, "you don't want to actually dress like a person from the 1940s."

Fans of the "rule of thirds" admit that some mental recalibration is needed to adopt the technique. "It does feel a bit odd the first time you do it," said Lane, the high-school teacher. But now that he's in the high-waisted club, he says he can't go back. "I just wore a pair of lower waisted, slim-fitting pants that I always thought looked great," he said. But after seeing himself in photos, Lane realized those low-slung pants now seemed dated. "I've changed gears. They just felt wrong."

Dozens of people rallied outside the Michigan headquarters of WK Kellogg Co. Tuesday, demanding that the company remove artificial dyes from its breakfast cereals in the U.S.

Kellogg, the maker of Froot Loops and Apple Jacks, announced nearly a decade ago that it would remove artificial colors and ingredients from its products by 2018.

The company has done that in other countries. In Canada, for example, Froot Loops are colored with concentrated carrot juice, watermelon juice and blueberry juice. But in the U.S., the cereal still contains artificial colors and BHT, a chemical preservative.

On Tuesday, activists said they were delivering petitions with more than 400,000 signatures asking WK Kellogg to remove artificial dyes and BHT from their cereals. Protesters said there was evidence that artificial dyes can contribute to behavioral issues in children.

“I’m here for all the mothers who struggle to feed their kids healthy food without added chemicals,” said Vani Hari, a food activist who previously pressured Kraft Heinz to remove artificial dyes from its macaroni and cheese.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration says it has reviewed and evaluated the effects of color additives on children’s behavior but believes that most children have no adverse effects when consuming them.

Battle Creek, Michigan-based WK Kellogg became a separate company last year when its snack division was spun off to form Kellanova. Kellanova kept the company’s international cereal business; it now makes Froot Loops with natural dyes for markets like Australia and the United Kingdom.

WK Kellogg said Tuesday that its foods are safe and all of its ingredients comply with federal regulations.

“Today, more than 85% of our cereal sales contain no colors from artificial sources,” the company said in a statement. “We continuously innovate new cereals that do not contain colors from artificial sources across our biggest brands, offering a broad choice of nourishing foods for our consumers.”

Kellogg said it announced its plan to remove artificial colors and ingredients almost a decade ago because it believed customers were seeking foods with natural ingredients and would welcome the change. But the company said it found that consumer preferences differed widely across markets.

“For example, there is better reception to our cereal recipes that utilize natural-color alternatives within the Canadian market than in the U.S.,” the company said.

Still, Kellogg may have to reconsider. Last month, Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom of California signed a bill banning six food dyes from food served in the state’s public schools, making it the first state in the U.S. to take such a step.

California’s law bans four of the dyes now used in Froot Loops: Red Dye No. 40, Yellow Dye No. 5, Yellow Dye No. 6 and Blue Dye No. 1.

Days after four people died in a school shooting in Georgia, students walked into middle-school principal Kirsten Clemons’s office and showed her a TikTok post they thought threatened their Missouri school.

As she tried to figure out whether the threat was real, Clemons’s phone soon began ringing with calls from concerned parents, teachers and neighboring principals who had seen the post.

“There became this panic,” Clemons said. “People were saying, ‘We’re next.’”

Threats of shootings, bombings and other violence are upending the school year throughout the country, fueling worry among families and frantic responses from law enforcement and district administrators. Most of the threats—which number roughly in the thousands, according to state and local estimates—have been hoaxes spread by teenagers on TikTok and Snapchat. Yet some threats have led to student arrests, canceled classes and football games, and drops in attendance.

School shootings like the Sept. 4 tragedy in Winder, Ga., which left two students and two teachers dead, often spawn a rise in copycat threats. But school leaders and security experts say the volume now is particularly high, driven in large part by how fast posts travel on social media. While some posts have detailed specific plans to attack a local school, many have been vague, like one mentioning “MHS,” which sparked alarm in several states with high schools using that acronym.

A Missouri hotline has fielded 301 reports of potential school violence this academic year, closing in on the amount reported in the entire prior year. Tennessee’s Department of Safety and Homeland Security investigated 321 threats from August to mid-September. Oklahoma City Police said they have looked into 65 reports of threats to metro-area schools since the school year began, many of them rumors or widely circulating social-media posts. Each one requires its own thorough inquiry to determine whether schools are in real danger.

“You cannot afford to say, ‘Eh, it’s not going to happen here,’” said Chad Soupir, a middle-school principal in suburban Omaha, Neb., who recently spent several days quashing a false rumor that a student was planning to shoot up the school after being romantically spurned by a classmate. “You want to make sure you have vetted it out completely.”

‘This is not a joke’

Today’s students have grown up in an era of school shootings and frequent lockdown drills that simulate what to do when an armed intruder is on campus. In many places, teachers are equipped with panic buttons, classroom doors stay locked and alarms sound if exterior doors are left propped open.

“We’re living in a society where it doesn’t matter if your school has actually suffered a tragedy like a shooting, almost every single student has had fears for their safety,” said Anjali Verma, a high-school senior in Pennsylvania, who speaks frequently about student mental health as president of the National Student Council.

Schools are on high alert at any online post even hinting at violence. Those caught posting hoax threats often say they meant it as a joke or a dare, say school administrators and law enforcement.

“We do communicate very often and let kids know this is not a joke,” said Howard Hepburn, the superintendent of Broward County Public Schools, the Florida district where 17 students and staff died in the 2018 shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School.

At least nine students in Broward County between the ages of 11 and 15 have been arrested for making threats since August. Most told law enforcement they meant the threats as a joke, according to a sheriff’s office news release, with one 13-year-old saying he was upset about a new school cellphone policy.

School leaders say they want students to know that hoax threats can lead to expulsion and even arrests, with felony charges in some places.

Teenagers make mistakes, but “spending all our resources and time and energy on potential threats should not be the focus of education,” said Brad Herzer, an assistant superintendent in Oklahoma City Public Schools.

‘A level of fear’

At Clemons’s Kansas City, Mo., district, the safety team soon realized the worrisome TikTok post wasn’t referring to their school, Lakeview Middle School, at all. It wasn’t even a threat. Instead, it was a cropped list of Georgia schools targeted by that state’s education department for extra academic help.

Yet a post showing the words “targeted” and “Lakeview Middle School” in the same frame was all it took to send alarm pulsing through Clemons’s community, where two years ago a gun was found in a student’s locker.

Almost as soon as Clemons assured students and parents that the Lakeview Middle School post wasn’t a real threat, she said she had to investigate and tell families about online posts from students who threatened gun violence against each other.

Clemons has seen safety threats ebb and flow in her years as a school leader. The Georgia shooting sent her community into a greater panic than she had experienced before.

“There is a level of fear in parents when they send their kid off to school,” she said.

Federal judges in Manhattan face daily frights like angry litigants, overzealous prosecutors and the specter of being reversed by an influential appeals court. But nothing prepares them for Art the Clown. 

“Watch out for that saw there,” top courthouse executive Edward Friedland said last week, pointing to the bloody animatronic figure of a hacksaw-wielding demonic mime. “It almost took off Judge Rakoff’s head.” 

U.S. District Judge Jed Rakoff is one of 10 jurists deciding the scariest of the thousands of proceedings held annually in the Southern District of New York: the courthouse administration’s annual Halloween competition.  

Once a year, the normally staid government office of audiovisual staffers, building architects, budget crunchers and court reporters is engulfed in fake blood, animatronic figures and strobe lights. What started as a workplace teambuilding exercise has turned into a cut-throat competition, presided over by district, magistrate and appellate judges from the Second U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.   

The proceedings are no joke. “I watched ‘Scream’ again this weekend,” said U.S. District Judge Jessica G. L. Clarke, who examined the office’s spooky tableus–twice–trailed by her law clerks. “I had to do my research beforehand.”  

The contest is the brainchild of Friedland, who for 15 years has served as the district executive for the Southern District’s courthouses, home to some of the highest-profile legal proceedings in the U.S.  

On recent dockets: corruption charges against New York City Mayor Eric Adams; the sex-trafficking prosecution of Sean “Diddy” Combs; litigation between writer E. Jean Carroll and former President Donald Trump; and the multibillion-dollar fraud trial of crypto wunderkind Sam Bankman-Fried.  

“It’s serious all day long,” said Friedland. 

Until Halloween, that is. Earlier this month, the mild-mannered Friedland moved his personal collection of 15 lifesize horror-movie animatronics into the district executive’s office suite. The administrator says the contest, now in its second year, boosts morale, surfaces his staff’s untapped talents and brings people together in a workplace where keeping the wheels of justice turning is serious business. 

His staff say their boss just really loves horror movies and seasonal decorations. 

“In his heart of hearts he’s a little kid who wants to have fun with his colleagues,” said William Jarrett, who manages courtroom technology. “He gets really excited when something big happens in the courthouse. And he gets really excited by Halloween.” 

Rakoff, the judge, offered another dissent. “Since Ed has to deal with more than 40 judges, he knows what monsters are really like,” he said. 

This year, five teams of staffers drew straws to determine their assigned scene locations and movie characters: Frankenstein; Ghostface from “Scream”; Chucky from “Child’s Play”; Beetlejuice; and Art the Clown from “Terrifier.” 

Once the assignments were set, the staff were blasé at work, but plotted elaborate horror tableaus at home, said architect Sheila Henriquez, a member of the Beetlejuice team.  “Everybody is like, ‘I don’t know yet what we’re doing,’” said Enriquez. “You don’t want to play your hand.” 

On the designated setup day, the offices transformed into a series of eerie movie scenes. 

Ghostface, with a bloody knife in hand, loomed over a mannequin dressed as Drew Barrymore and her duct-taped boyfriend in a lawn chair. The employee break room housed a lumbering Frankenstein with motion sensors, strobe lights and yellow caution tape. Around the corner, the house from Beetlejuice popped up across from the desk of Friedland’s executive assistant. 

Art the Clown guarded a supply closet where bloody garbage bags hung from the ceiling and stray plastic body parts mingled with Post-it notes and staples.  

“I walked in and thought I was in the wrong place,” said bankruptcy court clerk Vito Genna, who had come to the office for a meeting. 

Constructing horror scenes in an office isn’t easy. The Scream team initially installed a fog machine in a cardboard oven, to mimic the burning Jiffy Pop in the movie’s opening scene. After the machine malfunctioned, the team placed an electric tea kettle on the cardboard stove. 

“It completely caved in right before a judge came to view it,” said Alexa Fisher, the executive assistant. “We had to glue it really quick.” 

They settled for smell over smoke. “Butter-scented candle on Amazon,” added Fisher.  

The three women of the Beetlejuice group created the movie’s striped sandworm by stuffing a plastic bag with leftover shredded paper. Midway through construction, courthouse custodians took away the shreds, potentially dooming the unfinished worm to the recycling.  One team member reclaimed the shreds by sprinting down the hallway yelling, “Wait, wait!”  

The verdict is expected to be announced later this week. The judges send Friedland their rankings and any relevant opinions. The executive then calculates the winners, whose prizes include gift cards plus a full year of bragging rights. 

In evaluating the scenes, judges said they weigh elements including creativity, creepiness and attention to detail. Many involve their law clerks in the deliberations. 

Rakoff, known for his bold legal rulings on matters ranging from corporate crime to the death penalty, found a gumball machine in the Scream tableau particularly frightening. When he turned the handle, out popped a round plastic bubble containing a shiny sticker of the 81-year-old jurist’s likeness juxtaposed with Ghostface. “I don’t know if I’ll ever be as traumatized as I was then,” Rakoff said. 

Clarke said she is particularly attuned to details, like a waiver posted in front of the door that led to the Frankenstein scene. “All references to Monster Insanity in this Liability Waiver and Release (the ‘Release’), shall mean employees of the District Executive Office,” the waiver said. It then indemnified the office from all claims and attorney’s fees. 

The judge also had a soft spot for the Terrorizer team’s gory closet. “The candy dish with bones was a very nice touch,” she said.

Morgan Rae Playle was 27 when she crossed the threshold into adulthood. She started texting with uppercase letters. Just like getting a driver’s license or going off to college, turning on auto-capitalization for text messages has become a milestone of adulting. Even smartphone natives who have been thumb-typing since diapers know that true adults start sentences with capital letters, and that names and other proper nouns deserve the same. The question for many 20-somethings now is: When will society expect me to adhere to the laws of grammar? Some realize it’s time to turn on auto-capitalization when they begin texting with bosses and colleagues for work, given lowercase letters can be susceptible to misinterpretation. This is especially the case when communicating with older generations who didn’t grow up DMing their BFFs. But shunning the Shift key helps others cling to their youth. To them, a lowercase letter isn’t just a lowercase letter. Instead, it’s a way to forever remain cool and casual in texts. Even some CEOs do it. Lexicographers agree. They say lowercase typing isn’t laziness. It actually takes effort, since auto-capitalization is generally on by default. Like emojis and exclamation points, this is one of the many ways in which people try to get their humanness to shine through cold technical interfaces. Morgan typed in lowercase throughout her 20s, feeling it gave off a kind of carefree mimosa-brunch vibe. In her previous role as social-media strategist, she occasionally tweeted in lowercase. She started a new job last November in Dallas where she works on events and coordinates with clients and vendors. She didn’t want them to see messages in all lowercase and think an intern was texting them. So she turned on auto-capitalization. Capital letters are more sophisticated and buttoned-up—attributes she thinks are important to convey as she develops in the new role. The shift away from all lowercase might seem minor or silly to some people, but it’s significant for Morgan. It represents a decade of her life that’s now over. “I’ve grown out of the all-lowercase era,” she says. silly or friendly? Emilie Mosner, an 18-year-old high-school senior in Lancaster, Pa., turned off auto-capitalization on her phone when she hit ninth grade and joined her school’s swarm of Snapchatters. As she started applying to part-time jobs and talking to college recruiters a year ago, she decided it was time to turn capitalization back on. A few friends immediately asked why her tone became so formal. When Emilie explained her motivation, they too realized they’d soon be ditching the lowercase life. “I just feel like it would be silly because I’m trying to look presentable,” she says. “We’re going into the next phases of our life.” Some people might consider writing in all lowercase letters to be slacking. But it shouldn’t be interpreted that way, says Grant Barrett, head of lexicography at Dictionary.com. It’s meant to signal familiarity. Much like using italics, writing in all lowercase is a way to recreate spoken language, he says. “There’s always something else happening there, and usually the message is something important like, ‘I see you as a friend that I can be informal with.’” The poet E.E. Cummings famously wrote in lowercase. These days, popular young performers such as Olivia Rodrigo and Billie Eilish have lowercase song titles. Spotify jumped on the bandwagon with playlists labeled “teen beats” and “my life is a movie.” never grow up Caitlin Kurzman, a graduate student studying digital social media at University of Southern California in Los Angeles, generally uses only lowercase with her friends. She sees it as a more relaxed, low-pressure way of texting. The 23-year-old likes to think she’ll never turn on auto-capitalization, even after she graduates and gets a demanding job. “Honestly, I don’t want to,” she says. “I like the informality.” But Caitlin says she can’t always avoid uppercase—particularly in email. She has to remember to use the Shift key when responding to professors. Many millennial adults, well into their 30s, refuse to use capitalization. Sam Altman, chief executive of OpenAI, is known for mostly tweeting in lowercase. His capital-letter avoidance hasn’t prevented him from running one of the most powerful companies in the world. Drew Coffman, a 35-year-old social-media strategist in Los Angeles, stopped using proper capitalization around 2021. During the pandemic, people quarantined at home and gravitated toward being online. Drew realized he didn’t have to be so proper anymore, he says. He felt that capitalizing his tweets made them seem too formal, more like LinkedIn posts. “It just became clear there were a lot of benefits in being a human being online and not trying to be overly polished,” he says.

In the world of fashion, where trends come and go, one principle has stood the test of time: the Rule of Thirds. This age-old concept, rooted in geometry and art, has recently resurfaced in Hollywood and on TikTok as a style hack for men looking to appear taller. But what exactly is the Rule of Thirds, and how can you incorporate it into your wardrobe? Let’s break it down. Understanding the Rule of Thirds The Rule of Thirds is a design principle that divides an image into nine equal parts using two equally spaced horizontal lines and two equally spaced vertical lines. The idea is that by aligning a subject with these lines or their intersections, you create more tension, energy, and interest in the composition. In fashion, this translates to dividing your body into thirds rather than halves, which can create the illusion of height. Fashion stylist and TikTok influencer, Alex Monroe, explains, "The Rule of Thirds is all about proportions. By visually breaking your body into thirds, you can elongate your frame and create a more balanced look. It’s a trick that’s been used by stylists for years, but it’s gaining popularity now thanks to social media." Applying the Rule of Thirds to Your Wardrobe To apply the Rule of Thirds to your wardrobe, focus on how your clothing divides your body. The goal is to avoid cutting your body in half, which can make you appear shorter. Instead, aim for a 1:2 ratio, where one-third of your body is covered by one piece of clothing and the remaining two-thirds by another. 1. High-Waisted Trousers: High-waisted trousers are a great way to implement the Rule of Thirds. By raising the waistline, you create a longer leg line. "High-waisted pants can be a game-changer," says Monroe. "They draw the eye upward and give the illusion of longer legs, which is key to looking taller." 2. Cropped Jackets: Pairing high-waisted trousers with a cropped jacket can further enhance the effect. The shorter jacket stops at the waist, emphasizing the longer line of the legs. "Cropped jackets are perfect for creating that one-third top, two-thirds bottom ratio," Monroe adds. 3. Monochromatic Outfits: Wearing a single color from head to toe can also help elongate your frame. This creates a continuous line, making you appear taller. Fashion expert and author, Lisa Jacobs, notes, "Monochromatic outfits are not only stylish but also effective in creating a streamlined silhouette. They’re a simple way to apply the Rule of Thirds without overthinking it." 4. Vertical Stripes: Vertical stripes naturally draw the eye up and down, enhancing the illusion of height. Whether it’s a pinstriped suit or a vertically striped shirt, this pattern is a classic choice for those looking to appear taller. "Vertical stripes are a timeless pattern that works wonders for elongating the body," says Jacobs. Hollywood and TikTok: The New Frontiers The resurgence of the Rule of Thirds in men’s fashion can be attributed to its adoption by Hollywood celebrities and its viral spread on TikTok. Stars like Timothée Chalamet and Harry Styles have been spotted sporting outfits that cleverly use this principle, inspiring fans to try it themselves. On TikTok, fashion influencers are sharing tips and tricks on how to apply the Rule of Thirds, making it accessible to a wider audience. "Social media has democratized fashion," Monroe explains. "People are more willing to experiment with their style when they see others doing it online." Final Thoughts The Rule of Thirds is a simple yet effective way to enhance your style and create the illusion of height. By focusing on proportions and using clothing to divide your body into thirds, you can achieve a more balanced and elongated look. Whether you’re inspired by Hollywood or TikTok, this fashion hack is easy to incorporate into your wardrobe. As Jacobs concludes, "Fashion is all about expressing yourself and feeling confident. The Rule of Thirds is just one tool in your style arsenal. Use it to your advantage and have fun with it." So, next time you’re getting dressed, remember the Rule of Thirds. It might just be the secret to looking taller and feeling more confident in your style.

Outside the Michigan headquarters of WK Kellogg Co., a lively protest took place with dozens of demonstrators calling for the elimination of artificial dyes from the company's well-known cereals, such as Froot Loops. The demonstration, put together by worried consumers and health supporters, emphasized increasing worries about the possible health dangers linked to artificial food dyes.

At the forefront was Vani Hari, a prominent food activist and writer, who has consistently advocated for openness and better ingredients in the food sector. "Artificial dyes are associated with hyperactivity in children and various health problems," Hari asserted with conviction. "Kellogg should focus on consumer health rather than the visual appeal of its products."

The demonstration occurs as artificial food additives face growing examination in the United States. Although certain nations have prohibited or limited specific synthetic dyes, these substances are still commonly found in numerous American food items. Opponents claim that these additives are superfluous and may pose risks, particularly to children.

California's Governor, Gavin Newsom, has also voiced his backing for the initiative advocating for clearer food labeling. "Consumers deserve transparency about food ingredients and the ability to request safer options," Newsom stated recently. "Businesses such as Kellogg can set an example by offering more nutritious choices for families."

The demonstrators are calling on Kellogg to emulate other leading food companies that have started removing artificial colors due to consumer pressure. Lately, companies such as General Mills and Kraft have taken major steps to remove artificial dyes from their products.

Kellogg, on the other hand, insists that its products meet safety requirements and adhere to all regulations. In a response to the demonstration, the company highlighted its dedication to maintaining quality and safety. "We prioritize consumer feedback and are always looking for ways to enhance our products," the statement indicated. "Our cereals comply with all FDA standards, and we are dedicated to offering safe and healthy choices for our consumers."

Even with these reassurances, the demonstrators continue to stand firm in their demands. "We will persist until genuine change is achieved," declared a protester, clutching a sign that said, "Ditch the Dyes, Kellogg!" The protest ended with an appeal for consumers across the country to participate in the cause by expressing their concerns to the company and choosing brands that focus on natural ingredients.

With the ongoing discussion about artificial food additives, companies such as Kellogg are expected to face increasing pressure to align with evolving consumer demands. At present, the demonstrators aim for their actions to initiate a wider dialogue on food safety and transparency, eventually resulting in healthier options for everyone.

Since the beginning of the 2023-24 academic year, hundreds of schools nationwide have faced what law enforcement calls "swatting" incidents – false reports of active shooters or imminent threats designed to provoke large-scale emergency responses.

"We're seeing a disturbing trend where these hoax threats have increased by nearly 300% compared to the same period last year," says Kenneth Trump, president of National School Safety and Security Services. "What makes this particularly concerning is the sophistication of these threats and their coordinated nature."

The impact on school communities has been substantial. In October alone, more than 30 school districts across 14 states reported hoax threats, resulting in lockdowns, evacuations, and canceled activities. At Highland High School in Salt Lake City, a false shooting threat led to a 40% drop in attendance the following week, while a series of hoax calls in Michigan forced the cancellation of several Friday night football games.

Dr. Amanda Nickerson, director of the Alberti Center for Bullying Abuse Prevention at the University at Buffalo, explains the psychological toll: "Even when students know it's likely a hoax, these threats create genuine trauma. The uncertainty and repeated disruptions can lead to increased anxiety, decreased focus on learning, and a persistent sense of insecurity."

Law enforcement agencies and school administrators are taking these threats seriously, regardless of their authenticity. FBI Special Agent Marcus Williams notes, "Each threat requires a full emergency response. We can't afford to assume any threat is false, which strains resources and can impact our ability to respond to real emergencies."

The consequences for those making these threats are severe. Since September, at least 27 students nationwide have been arrested for making false threats, facing charges that can include making terroristic threats, disrupting public schools, and cyber harassment. Many of these students are discovering that what they considered a prank can result in felony charges and potential prison time.

"We're seeing students as young as 12 facing serious criminal charges," says District Attorney Sarah Chen of Los Angeles County. "What they don't realize is that these actions can follow them well into adulthood, affecting college applications and future employment opportunities."

Schools are responding with enhanced security measures and communication protocols. The National Association of School Resource Officers reports that 78% of member schools have updated their emergency response procedures this year, while 65% have implemented new systems for verifying threats.

"We've had to become more sophisticated in how we assess and respond to threats," explains Dr. Robert Martinez, superintendent of a large suburban Chicago school district. "We're using artificial intelligence tools to track online threats and working closely with local law enforcement to verify credibility quickly."

Parents are also feeling the strain. Sarah Thompson, a mother of two high school students in Atlanta, describes the emotional toll: "Every time my phone buzzes with a school alert, my heart stops. Even though most threats turn out to be false, the fear is very real."

Experts suggest several factors contributing to the increase in hoax threats. Dr. Lisa Strohman, a clinical psychologist specializing in digital technology's impact on youth, points to social media's role: "We're seeing these threats spread through platforms like TikTok and Snapchat, where students might be motivated by the attention or disruption they can cause. The anonymity of digital platforms makes it easier for individuals to make threats without immediately facing consequences."

School districts are now focusing on prevention through education. Many have implemented digital citizenship programs and are working to help students understand the severity of making false threats.

"Education is key," says Michael Harrison, a school safety consultant. "We're teaching students about digital footprints and how online actions have real-world consequences. We're also encouraging them to report suspicious behavior through anonymous reporting systems."

Looking ahead, experts emphasize the need for a coordinated response involving law enforcement, school administrators, mental health professionals, and technology companies. The Department of Homeland Security has announced plans to provide additional resources and training to schools for threat assessment and response.

"This isn't just a school problem or a law enforcement problem," says Dr. Elizabeth Reeves, an educational policy researcher at Georgetown University. "It requires a community-wide approach to address the underlying issues that lead students to make these threats in the first place."

As schools continue to navigate this challenge, the focus remains on maintaining safe learning environments while addressing the psychological impact on students and staff. With improved protocols, enhanced communication systems, and stronger partnerships between schools and law enforcement, administrators hope to reduce the frequency and impact of these disruptive threats.

"Our primary goal is ensuring students feel safe at school," concludes Dr. Martinez. "We can't let these threats, real or fake, undermine the fundamental purpose of education: providing a secure environment where learning can flourish."

Tossing a few capital letters into an email might seem trivial, but try telling that to a generation raised on text messages, TikTok captions, and Slack threads that never bother with the shift key. Now that these individuals are moving deeper into the workforce, some are feeling a new kind of pressure: the expectation that they present themselves in writing as adults—capital letters and all.

At a mid-sized marketing agency in Minneapolis, brand strategist Amanda Farrell recalls a tense moment last December when a new hire’s email arrived looking more like a casual group text than a professional note. “He wrote: ‘hey team, gonna run these numbers by tom. b right back.’ I didn’t know whether to laugh or panic,” she says. Her manager hinted that such informality wasn’t a big deal for Slack or text messages among peers, but that email should reflect “grownup” formatting. Farrell says the new hire got the message. The next morning he replied with a follow-up: “Hey Team, I’ll be sending the updated metrics shortly.” She almost imagined him wincing as he typed the capital “H” in “Hey.”

Plenty of veterans in corporate offices have seen email styles evolve over the decades. Early internet correspondences bristled with ALL CAPS subject lines and chaotic punctuation. Then came a period of pristine professionalism—subject lines carefully cased, salutations and sign-offs neatly aligned. Younger workers influenced by social media norms often find the shift key optional, assuming that as long as the content is clear, nobody cares about capitalization.

But many people do. “Workplace communication is a dance we’re all still learning, and typography is a step in that dance,” says Susan Brenner, a communications professor at Northwestern University’s School of Communication. Brenner studies how nonverbal cues translate into digital text formats. “Capitalization signals formality, respect, and a willingness to play by longstanding rules,” she says. “This is not a small thing. It’s not an empty ritual. It’s a way to say, ‘I take this interaction seriously.’”

At a tech startup in Austin, Texas, product manager Colin Ray spent his first six months typing everything in lowercase. He admits he simply never formed the habit of using caps beyond the occasional “LOL.” When a senior colleague gently reminded him that investors sometimes get looped in on email chains, he decided to adjust. “It felt weird at first,” Ray says. “I typed like i always do, and then i went back and forced myself to fix the capitalization. After a few weeks, it got easier.” Still, he confesses that if he’s just messaging a close teammate on Slack, he might revert to all lowercase. “It’s like wearing a nice shirt when you’re meeting a client, and a T-shirt when you’re just talking to your buddy who sits next to you,” he says.

Not everyone is ready to give in. There are holdouts who see the insistence on capitalization as fussy. “I think it’s elitist,” says Lucy Tran, a graphic designer in Brooklyn who works remotely for a fashion brand. She rarely capitalizes her first-person pronoun “I,” and her memos bristle with a certain free-flowing style: “hey dmitri, got the new mockups—will push them after lunch.” Her boss hasn’t complained, and Tran sees her lowercase approach as a signature, a subtle stand against conformity. “I don’t think uppercase letters are going to make my ideas better or clearer,” she says. “If the content is good, who cares if i capitalized the first letter of the sentence?”

Some managers feel caught in the middle, not wanting to sound like old-school grammar police while still maintaining some semblance of professionalism. A human resources director at a Philadelphia insurance firm—who asked not to be named because she’s still navigating these norms—says her team had a formal discussion last fall. They concluded that internal Slack messages could remain casual, but external emails and especially client reports should reflect standard writing conventions, including capitalization. “We decided it’s like dressing business-casual in person,” she explains. “No one’s asking you to wear a three-piece suit, but sweatpants are out.”

The pressure to appear “grownup” in writing isn’t just about aesthetics. Some believe that older clients might subconsciously question the competence of a person who can’t manage a capital “I” or the first letter of a brand’s name. “The risk is subtle,” says Tom Davenport, a freelance consultant who advises small businesses on branding. “A CEO reading a pitch deck might not say out loud, ‘This person can’t capitalize their letters, I’m dropping their proposal.’ But tiny signals add up. We all know presentation matters. It’s not just what you say; it’s how you say it—even how you type it.”

A few companies have turned this into a running joke. In May, a media startup in Seattle reportedly created a Slack channel called #caps-training to help interns adjust their writing style before sending emails to advertisers. According to one staffer, participants teased each other, awarding virtual “gold stars” for correctly capitalized sentences. The idea was to remove tension and turn learning a small professional skill into a game. “We had kids fresh out of college who wrote beautifully, but looked like they were texting their roommates,” the staffer says. “A few rounds of good-natured ribbing later, everybody was typing like they’d been doing it forever.”

This subtle shift may never feel entirely natural to some. But, as Brenner at Northwestern points out, language always changes, and so do its norms. “A generation from now, maybe everything is lowercase, and we’ll look back at uppercase letters as this strange relic,” she says. “For now, though, in many offices, using proper capitalization can feel like a low-stakes rite of passage—a small signal that you’ve arrived.”
